usage: 평범하다 = ordinary, a very common pairing
I want to become an office worker.
examples: 저는 회사원이에요.
I'm an office worker.
the default polite way to state your job
우리 형은 은행에서 일하는 회사원이에요.
My older brother is an office worker at a bank.
에서 marks the workplace where the action happens
회사원들은 보통 아침 아홉 시까지 출근해요.
Office workers usually clock in by nine in the morning.
출근하다 'go to work' is the verb that lives with 회사원
nuance: 회사원 is 會社員 ('company-member'), literally a member of a company, and it is the neutral catch-all a salaried employee of a private firm gives when asked 무슨 일 하세요? Contrast it with 직장인, which means 'a working person' in general (anyone with a paid job, including teachers or nurses): every 회사원 is a 직장인, but not every 직장인 is a 회사원. Also separate it from 사업가, the owner who runs the business — a 회사원 is employed by someone else. The pitfall for English speakers is twofold: 회사원 ends in a consonant so the copula is 회사원이에요, never 'office worker'-style 회사원예요; and don't translate 'I work at a company' as a job title — to name the job you simply say 회사원이에요 rather than literally rendering the English sentence.

usage: 이에요 after the consonant ending 원
공무원 시험 is a fixed compound; 시험을 보다 = sit an exam
I want to become a civil servant.
examples: 저는 공무원이에요.
I'm a civil servant.
stated plainly, like any job
우리 누나는 시청에서 일하는 공무원이에요.
My older sister is a civil servant working at city hall.
시청 'city hall' is a typical 공무원 workplace
요즘 젊은 사람들이 공무원 시험을 많이 준비해요.
These days many young people study for the civil-service exam.
준비하다 'prepare for' is the verb that collocates with 시험
nuance: 공무원 is 公務員 ('public-affairs-member'), one who handles 공무, the affairs of the state, so it covers anyone employed by the government — a ward office clerk, a public-school teacher, a tax officer. The key contrast is with 회사원: a 회사원 works for a private 회사, while a 공무원 works for the 나라 (state) and has 정년 (guaranteed tenure to retirement). Don't confuse it with 정치인 (a politician, who is elected) — a 공무원 is hired through the 공무원 시험 and is meant to be politically neutral. For learners the pitfalls are the copula (consonant ending → 공무원이에요, not 공무원예요) and the cultural weight: in Korea 공무원 is prized for 안정성 (stability), so saying 공무원이 되고 싶어요 carries a strong 'I want a secure life' overtone that the bare English 'civil servant' doesn't convey.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 부
전업 'sole occupation' stresses it is full-time work
집안일 'household chores' is the typical object
examples: 우리 엄마는 주부예요.
My mom is a homemaker.
the most natural everyday sentence with 주부
저는 아이를 키우는 전업주부예요.
I'm a full-time homemaker raising children.
키우다 'raise (a child)' collocates with 주부
요즘은 주부도 부업으로 돈을 벌어요.
These days homemakers also earn money with a side job.
부업 'side work' shows 주부 is treated as real labor
nuance: 주부 is 主婦 ('head-wife'), the person who is the 主 (head, manager) of household affairs; historically it implies a married woman running the home. The sharp modern contrast is 전업주부 (full-time homemaker, no outside job) versus 맞벌이 (a dual-income couple where both work) — and note the rising 주부 covers men too, though many will specify 전업주부 or use 살림하다 'to keep house' for the activity. Don't confuse 주부 (the person) with 가사 / 집안일 (the housework itself). usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
I want to become a businessperson.
examples: 우리 삼촌은 사업가예요.
My uncle is a businessperson.
stating someone's occupation plainly
그분은 작은 회사를 세운 사업가예요.
He's a businessperson who founded a small company.
세우다 'establish (a company)' collocates with 사업가
성공한 사업가가 되려면 위험을 감수해야 해요.
To become a successful businessperson you have to take risks.
위험을 감수하다 'bear risk' captures the core of 사업가
nuance: 사업가 is 事業家 ('enterprise-expert'), where 가(家) is the suffix for a person skilled in a field (as in 작가, 화가, 음악가); it pictures someone who builds and runs an 사업 (a business venture) and shoulders its risk. Contrast three near words: 사업가 = the entrepreneur/operator with vision and risk; 사장(님) = the literal 'company president/boss' title you address people by; and 자영업자 = a small self-employed shop owner. So a corner-store owner is rarely called a 사업가 — that word sounds bigger, more ambitious. Don't mix 사업가 (the person) with 사업 (the business itself: 사업을 하다 'run a business'). Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel so it's 사업가예요, never 사업가이에요; and don't borrow English 'I do business' literally as a title — to name the job say 사업가예요.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 너
the field word goes in front: 옷/웹/그래픽 디자이너
I want to become a designer.
examples: 저는 디자이너예요.
I'm a designer.
the bare job statement
제 친구는 옷을 만드는 디자이너예요.
My friend is a designer who makes clothes.
the -는 clause 옷을 만드는 specifies the kind of designer
그 디자이너가 이번 시즌 신상품을 디자인했어요.
That designer designed this season's new products.
디자인하다 'to design' is the matching verb
nuance: 디자이너 is a direct loanword from English 'designer', written in 외래어 (foreign-loan) spelling, used for anyone who designs — clothes, graphics, web pages, products. Be careful not to confuse 디자이너 with 디자인 (the design itself: 디자인이 예쁘다 'the design is pretty') — one is the person, one is the output. A nearby word is 설계자, but that leans toward technical/architectural 'designer-engineer', so for fashion or visual work stick with 디자이너. Pitfalls for English speakers: 너 ends in a vowel, so it's 디자이너예요, never 디자이너이에요; and the matching verb is 디자인하다, so 'I design clothes' is 옷을 디자인해요, not a literal word-by-word transfer of the English.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 머
실력 있다 'have skill' is the natural praise
I want to become a programmer.
examples: 저는 프로그래머예요.
I'm a programmer.
the plain job answer
제 동생은 게임을 만드는 프로그래머예요.
My younger sibling is a programmer who makes games.
만들다 'make' describes what they build
프로그래머가 밤늦게까지 코드를 짜요.
The programmer writes code late into the night.
코드를 짜다 'write/assemble code' is the insider collocation
nuance: 프로그래머 is the loanword 'programmer', the person who writes computer 프로그램 (programs). The most useful contrast is with 개발자 ('developer', 開發者 'one who develops'): in real Korean tech workplaces 개발자 is now the more common, broader title (covering design, building, and shipping software), while 프로그래머 highlights specifically the coding act and can sound slightly narrower or more old-school. Both are fine to say. Don't confuse 프로그래머 (the person) with 프로그램 (the program) — you make a 프로그램, you are a 프로그래머. The natural verb for the work is 코드를 짜다 or 개발하다, not a literal calque of English 'to program'. Pitfall: 머 ends in a vowel, so it must be 프로그래머예요, never 프로그래머이에요.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 니어
the field goes in front, like 소프트웨어/기계 엔지니어
I want to become an engineer.
examples: 저는 엔지니어예요.
I'm an engineer.
the plain occupation statement
우리 형은 자동차를 만드는 엔지니어예요.
My older brother is an engineer who builds cars.
만들다 'build/make' describes the work
엔지니어가 고장 난 기계를 직접 고쳤어요.
The engineer fixed the broken machine himself.
고치다 'repair' pairs with hands-on engineering
nuance: 엔지니어 is the loanword 'engineer', someone who designs, builds, and maintains machines or systems. The instructive contrast is with the Sino-Korean 기술자 (技術者 'skill-person', a technician): 엔지니어 leans toward the degreed, design-and-theory professional, while 기술자 emphasizes a hands-on tradesperson who operates or repairs. So a factory line repairer might be a 기술자, whereas the person who designed the line is an 엔지니어 — though in casual speech they overlap. As with other fields, Koreans front the specialty: 기계 엔지니어, 소프트웨어 엔지니어. Pitfalls: 니어 ends in a vowel, so it's 엔지니어예요, never 엔지니어이에요; and don't reach for 'engineer' to mean a train driver (a false friend from older English) — that person is a 기관사.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
I want to become a writer.
examples: 저는 작가예요.
I'm a writer.
the bare job statement
그분은 소설을 쓰는 작가예요.
She's a writer who writes novels.
쓰다 'write' is the core verb of 작가
그 작가가 이번에 새 책을 냈어요.
That author just put out a new book.
책을 내다 'release a book' is the idiomatic phrase, not 만들다
nuance: 작가 is 作家 ('make-house/expert' = one who creates works), used for authors of novels, essays, and also drama or film scripts (a 드라마 작가 is a screenwriter). The crucial contrast for learners is 기자 (記者, a news reporter who reports facts) — both write, but 작가 creates literary/creative work while 기자 gathers and reports news, so never swap them. A wider umbrella is 글쓴이/저자 'author of a specific text', but as a profession 작가 is the word. Note the suffix 가(家) marks 'a master of a field', the same one in 화가, 사업가, 음악가. Pitfalls: 가 ends in a vowel → 작가예요, never 작가이에요; and the idiom for publishing is 책을 내다 (literally 'put out a book'), so don't calque English 'make a book' as 책을 만들다, which sounds like physically manufacturing it.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 가
유명하다 in its modifier form 유명한
I want to become a painter.
examples: 우리 이모는 화가예요.
My aunt is a painter.
naming someone's profession
그분은 풍경을 그리는 화가예요.
He's a painter who paints landscapes.
그리다 'draw/paint' is the verb that lives with 화가
그 화가가 그린 그림이 비싸게 팔렸어요.
The picture that painter made sold for a high price.
그림 'picture' is the product; note 그리다 not 만들다
nuance: 화가 is 畵家 ('picture-expert'), a fine-art painter whose work is 그림 (pictures/paintings), again with the 가(家) 'master of a field' suffix. The contrast to keep clear: 화가 is one specific kind of 예술가 (藝術家, artist) — 예술가 is the umbrella that also includes musicians (음악가), dancers, and sculptors, so a 화가 is an 예술가 but not vice versa. usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 수; said of oneself
add 님 + honorific 오시다 when speaking about them
께 is the honorific 'to'; 여쭤보다 humbly = ask
I want to become a professor.
examples: 저는 대학교에서 가르치는 교수예요.

about yourself you may drop 님
우리 교수님은 정말 친절하세요.
Our professor is really kind.
친절하시다: the honorific -시- because they outrank you
교수님이 오늘 어려운 질문을 하셨어요.

하셨어요 = honorific past of 하다 for a respected person

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 사
필요하다 'be needed' takes 이/가, not 을/를
I want to become an interpreter.
examples: 저는 통역사예요.
I'm an interpreter.
the plain job answer
회의에 통역사가 한 명 왔어요.
One interpreter came to the meeting.
명 is the counter for people
그 통역사가 영어를 한국어로 통역했어요.

A를 B로 통역하다 'interpret A into B'

It means specifically an interpreter of spoken language in real time. The essential contrast is 번역사 (翻譯士), who translates written text: spoken = 통역, written = 번역, and the people and verbs differ (통역하다 vs 번역하다). Don't blur them — saying 번역사 for a conference interpreter is a clear error to Korean ears. Note also the verb 통역하다 takes the pattern A를 B(으)로 통역하다. Pitfalls: 사 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 통역사예요, never 통역사이에요; and the thing you 'need' takes 이/가 with 필요하다 (통역사가 필요해요), not the 을/를 an English speaker expects from 'need an interpreter'.

usage: 예요 after the vowel ending 사
the vehicle goes in front: 버스/택시/트럭 운전사
기사 is the more courteous term you call them by
I want to become a driver.
examples: 우리 아버지는 트럭 운전사예요.
My father is a truck driver.
the vehicle precedes 운전사
택시 운전사가 길을 정말 잘 알아요.

Pitfalls: 사 ends in a vowel, so the copula is 운전사예요, never 운전사이에요; and for the activity 'I can drive' you say 운전할 수 있어요, using the verb 운전하다, not the job noun.
